title: As Ubuntu embraces AI, Debian discusses banning all AI-generated code
content:
Summary
- Debian opened a General Resolution to decide whether to allow AI-generated or AI-assisted code.
- Proposal A seeks to ban all LLM-generated and assisted code, citing copyright, quality, community, and ethics.
- Proposal B permits AI code if submitters declare usage, ensure copyright-free work, and take responsibility.
The rapid development of LLM coding tools has forced the open-source community to ask itself the question: does AI belong in the world of FOSS? How much AI belongs? Are AI-powered tools allowed? What about AI-generated code?
Ubuntu has already opened the gates for AI-powered snaps, but the topic of LLM-generated code is now on the docket for Debian. If one of the proposals passes, it should mean a huge shift in how Linux developers create code.
Debian moves to ban all AI-generated content
The alternative option isn't to allow vibe-coded software, though
Debian has officially opened up a General Resolution on the topic of AI-created code. There are two proposals: Proposal A aims to remove all AI-generated code, including AI-assisted code, while Proposal B wants to allow AI code with some caveats.
Proposal A starts strong:
                        Debian has a well-earned reputation for stability. This stability is crucial to Debian's position in the free software ecosystem. It is our belief that widespread LLM usage comes from the "move fast, and break things" attitude that, while common in many parts of this industry, is contrary to what makes Debian Debian, and is inappropriate for Debian contributors.
Proposal A cites four issues with using AI-generated code. The first is copyright; the post states that LLM code has an "unclear legal status" and that Debian would prefer code was submitted with clear copyright terms. The post says that human-generated code with murky copyright status is rejected, so LLM code should be no different.
The second is quality. Proposal A claims that "an LLM can never 'know' if its output is correct since it merely produces syntactically likely combinations of the training data," and that while that's "good enough" for general use, "In Debian, it is not." The proposal claims that an AI would not keep up with Debian's shifting guidelines and would resort to archived code that uses outdated practices.
The third is community. Proposal A states that Debian is very community-focused, and that "New contributors submitting LLM output for review places an unnecessary strain on the reviewer" and doesn't teach submitters how Debian works or how to code for it.
The fourth is ethics. Proposal A claims that LLM companies are unethical in their practices "by scraping the whole web for training data without any regard for license, copyright, or even established conventions such as robots.txt." It also points to agent activity causing an accidental DDoS attack against Debian in the past and cites issues with the environmental impact of data centers.
In the other corner, Proposal B seems to lay out something similar to how AI-generated code is handled on the Linux kernel. The proposal allows AI-generated code only if the submitter takes full accountability for it, ensures it's free of copyright issues, and declares any LLM usage.
The topic is currently being discussed, so we'll have to wait and see which way Debian will go in this new frontier.

report.summary: Debian considers banning AI-generated code via General Resolution, with Proposal A for total ban and Proposal B for conditional allowance.
report.background: Debian is debating whether AI-generated code belongs in its free software project. A General Resolution contains two proposals. Proposal A would ban all LLM-generated and AI-assisted code, citing copyright uncertainty, poor quality, reviewer strain, and ethical concerns about training data and environmental impact. Proposal B would allow AI code if submitters declare usage, take responsibility, and ensure copyright cleanliness, similar to the Linux kernel. The debate comes as Ubuntu embraces AI snaps, showing divergence among Linux distributions. LLM coding tools have rapidly matured, forcing FOSS communities to define rules for machine-assisted contributions.
key_points: Proposal A calls for a complete ban on LLM-generated and AI-assisted code. It argues that such code has unclear legal and copyright status, and that an LLM can never truly know if its output is correct, making it unfit for Debian's stability-focused development model.

Proposal B offers a conditional path: AI-generated code may be accepted if the submitter clearly declares any LLM usage, takes full accountability for the code, and verifies it is free of copyright issues. This mirrors how the Linux kernel handles AI contributions.

Debian's community concerns focus on maintainer workload. The proposal says new contributors submitting AI output simply place unnecessary strain on reviewers, and that the practice fails to teach newcomers Debian's standards, guidelines, or how to genuinely code for the project.

Ethical objections include LLM companies scraping the web without regard for license terms or robots.txt, earlier AI agent activity that accidentally caused a DDoS attack against Debian, and the environmental impact of data centers powering AI models.
report.impact: A Debian decision will resonate across the open-source ecosystem. If Proposal A passes, it could create a precedent for other conservative distributions and set a strict line between human and machine contributions, potentially slowing adoption of AI tools among FOSS maintainers. If Proposal B passes, it may encourage broader but responsible usage, with clear disclosure becoming standard. For developers, this highlights the importance of licensing and accountability when using LLM assistants. Regular users benefit from stable, well-reviewed code, but may see fewer cutting-edge AI integrations. The debate also pressures AI companies to improve training transparency and environmental practices.
report.tools: Readers can follow Debian's General Resolution discussion on the debian-vote mailing list and the Debian wiki. For those exploring AI-assisted FOSS development, tools like GitHub Copilot, OpenHands, and the Linux kernel's guidance on marking AI submissions provide useful context. Ubuntu's AI snaps and Snapcraft also show one side of this evolving debate.
